claims.text: Pico says the common arguments for human excellence left him unsatisfied, among them that man is only slightly inferior to the angels.

quotes.text: I was unsatisfied by the arguments put forward by many men to explain the excellence of human nature
and only slightly inferior, as David affirms, to the angels
ab angelis, teste Davide, paulo deminutum

claims.text: Pico allows that the common reasons for human dignity are not the principal ones, and asks why the angels and the blessed choirs of heaven should not be admired more.

quotes.text: These reasons are indeed great, but they are nonetheless not the principal ones
why then would we not find the angels themselves and the blessed choirs of heaven even more admirable
Cur enim non ipsos angelos et beatissimos caeli choros magis admiremur

claims.text: Pico says the condition that man received in the universal order is one to be envied by the beasts, by the stars and by the intelligences dwelling beyond this world.

quotes.text: a condition to be envied not only by beasts but even by the stars and the intelligences dwelling beyond this world
non brutis modo, sed astris, sed ultramundanis mentibus invidiosam

claims.text: In Pico's account of creation God had already adorned the supercelestial region with intelligences and given the heavenly globes eternal souls before man was made.

quotes.text: He had already adorned the supercelestial region with intelligences, enlivened the heavenly globes with eternal souls
Supercelestem regionem mentibus decorarat; ethereos globos aeternis animis vegetarat

claims.text: Pico says that when man was to be made every place in the world was already filled and had been assigned to the highest, the middle and the lowest orders.

quotes.text: nor was there among the seats of the world any place for this contemplator of the universe
Every place was by then filled; all things had already been assigned to the highest, the middle, and the lowest orders
Iam plena omnia; omnia summis, mediis infimisque ordinibus fuerant distributa

claims.text: Pico says the highest spirits, which the editors translate as Intelligences, are from the beginning or soon after what they will be for all eternity, whereas man may become what he wills.

quotes.text: The Intelligences have been, either from the beginning or soon thereafter, what they are perpetually going to be throughout eternity
Supremi spiritus aut ab initio aut paulo mox id fuerunt, quod sunt futuri in perpetuas aeternitates
O supreme liberality of God the Father, and supreme and wonderful happiness of man who is permitted to obtain what he desires and to be what he wills

claims.text: Pico says that a man who cultivates his intellectual seeds will be an angel and a son of God, just as cultivating the rational seeds makes him a heavenly being.

quotes.text: If he cultivates his rational seeds, he will become a heavenly being. If he cultivates his intellectual seeds, he will be an angel and a son of God
si rationalia, caeleste evadet animal; si intellectualia, angelus erit et Dei filius

judged.justification: The angelic state is the top of a scale of what man may cultivate in himself, not a separate order he can only envy.

claims.text: Pico says that a man dissatisfied with the lot of every creature who gathers himself into the centre of his unity becomes one spirit with God and is set above all things, going beyond the angelic state of section 29.

quotes.text: gathers himself into the centre of his own unity, thus becoming a single spirit with God in the solitary darkness of the Father, he, who had been placed above all things, will become superior to all things
et si, nulla creaturarum sorte contentus, in unitatis centrum suae se receperit, unus cum Deo spiritus factus, in solitaria Patris caligine

judged.justification: Makes the angel a stage on the way, not the goal: the final term is union with God in darkness.

claims.text: Pico says the most secret Hebrew theology transforms Enoch into an angel of divinity, named in Hebrew, and at other times reshapes other men into other spirits.

quotes.text: even the most secret Hebrew theology at one time transforms holy Enoch into an angel of divinity
whom they call [ מטטרון ] Metatron
and at other times it reshapes other men into other spirits

judged.justification: Fixes the Kabbalistic Enoch-Metatron transformation as the model of human-to-angelic change in the Oration.

claims.text: Pico says that what makes an angel is spiritual intelligence, not separation from the body.

quotes.text: not the circular body that makes the heavens, but straightforward reason; not the separation from the body that makes an angel, but its spiritual intelligence
nec caelum orbiculatum corpus, sed recta ratio; nec sequestratio corporis, sed spiritalis intelligentia angelum facit

judged.justification: Defines the angelic by a mode of knowing, so that an embodied philosopher can qualify.

claims.text: Pico ranks the philosopher of right reason as a heavenly creature, and the pure contemplator withdrawn into the mind as neither earthly nor heavenly but a still more eminent spirit in human flesh.

quotes.text: If you see a philosopher discerning things with right reason, worship him, for he is not an earthly creature, but divine

If you see a pure contemplator, oblivious to his body and absorbed in the recesses of his mind, this is neither an earthly nor a heavenly creature: this is a still more eminent spirit, clothed in human flesh

judged.justification: A rank above the heavenly creature of section 29, clothed in flesh.

claims.text: Pico urges his hearers to fly to the otherworldly court near the highest Divinity, where seraphim, cherubim and thrones hold the first places, and to emulate their dignity and glory without accepting second place.

quotes.text: let us fly off to the otherworldly court that is near to the most eminent Divinity

There, according to the sacred mysteries, seraphim, cherubim, and thrones occupy the first places; let us emulate their dignity and glory, unwilling as we are to yield to them and unable to endure second place
Ibi, ut sacra tradunt mysteria, Seraphin, Cherubin et Throni primas possident

judged.justification: Sets the emulation of the highest angels as the programme of the whole Oration.

claims.text: Pico says that by living the life the highest angels live, which man is able to do, we may not be inferior to them and may equal their lot.

quotes.text: If so we wish, we will not be inferior to them at all
Let us consider what they do, what life they lead
If we too live that life (and indeed we can), we will be equal to their lot

claims.text: Pico characterises the three ranks: the seraph burns with the fire of love, the cherub shines with the splendour of intelligence, the throne stands in the steadfastness of judgment.

quotes.text: The seraph burns with the fire of love; the cherub shines with the splendour of intelligence; the throne stands in the steadfastness of judgment
Ardet Saraph charitatis igne; fulget Cherub intelligentiae splendore; stat Thronus iudicii firmitate

judged.justification: Assigns each of the three ranks one operation, love, intelligence, judgment, on which the rest of the passage builds.

claims.text: Pico says that a man devoted to the active life and caring rightly for inferior things will be strengthened by the steadfast solidity of the thrones.

quotes.text: if we, being dedicated to an active life, undertake the care of inferior things with proper consideration of their worth, we will be strengthened by the steadfast solidity of the thrones
Igitur si actuosae addicti vitae inferiorum curam recto examine susceperimus, Thronorum stata soliditate firmabimur

claims.text: Pico says that a man released from action who meditates on the Creator in creation and on creation in the Creator will shine with cherubic light.

quotes.text: If we, being unburdened by actions, meditate on the Creator in His creation and on creation in the Creator, we shall be engaged in the tranquillity of contemplation; we shall shine on all sides with cherubic light
luce Cherubica undique corruscabimus

claims.text: Pico says that a man who burns with charity for the Creator alone will burst into flame in the likeness of the seraphim.

quotes.text: If we burn for the Creator alone, with charity, with its all-consuming fire, we shall burst into flame in the likeness of the seraphim
in Saraphicam effigiem repente flammabimur

claims.text: Pico says that God flies over the cherub, who is the contemplator, and imbues him with warmth as if brooding over him.

quotes.text: Over the cherub, that is, over the contemplator, He flies and, as if brooding over him, imbues him with warmth
Super Cherub, idest contemplatore, volat atque eum quasi incubando fovet

claims.text: Pico says that the seraph, who is a lover, is in God and God in him, so that he and God are one.

quotes.text: He who is a seraph, that is, a lover, is in God and God is in him; indeed, he and God are one
Qui Saraph, idest amator est, in Deo est, et Deus in eo, immo et Deus et ipse unum sunt

claims.text: Pico says that the power of the thrones is reached by judging and the height of the seraphim by loving, that neither judging nor loving is possible of things unknown, and gives Moses as the example who loved what he had seen and judged as a contemplator.

quotes.text: Great is the power of the thrones that we may reach by judging; supreme is the height of the seraphim that we may reach by loving
And yet in what manner can anyone either judge or love things unknown?
Moses loved the Lord Whom he saw. As a judge, Moses administered to the people the things that he earlier saw on the mountain as a contemplator

judged.justification: Argues that knowing must precede both loving and judging, which is what puts the cherub in the middle.

claims.text: Pico says the cherub, placed in the middle, prepares us by his light for the seraphic fire and illuminates the judgment of the thrones.

quotes.text: the cherub, located in the middle position, uses his light both to prepare us for the seraphic fire and likewise to illuminate for us the judgment of the thrones
Ergo medius Cherub sua luce et Saraphico igni nos praeparat, et ad Thronorum iudicium pariter illuminat

claims.text: Pico calls the cherub the bond of the Prime Minds, the order of Pallas and the overseer of contemplative philosophy, and says he is to be emulated first so that we may be raised to love and descend to action.

quotes.text: The cherub is the bond of the Prime Minds, the order of Pallas, the overseer of contemplative philosophy. First we must emulate him, thirst after him and to the same degree understand him in order that we may be raised from him to the heights of love and descend from him, well taught and prepared, to the duties of the active life
Hic est nodus primarum mentium, ordo Palladicus philosophiae contemplativae preses

judged.justification: Ties the cherub, the contemplative order and Pallas together, and puts philosophy at the cherubic middle of the ascent.

claims.text: Pico proposes to ask the apostle Paul, caught up to the third heaven, what the cherubic hosts do, and says Paul will answer in the words of Dionysius that they are cleansed, then illuminated, and afterward perfected.

quotes.text: Let us inquire of the apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, regarding the activities of the cherubic hosts whom he saw when raised up to the third heaven
He will certainly answer, according to the interpretation of Dionysius, that they are cleansed, then illuminated, and afterward are perfected

judged.justification: Grounds the three-stage way of the Oration in Dionysius on the cherubic hosts.

claims.text: Pico says that emulating the cherubic life on earth means purging the soul through moral science and dialectics, then bathing it in the light of natural philosophy so that it may be perfected by knowledge of divine things.

quotes.text: emulating the cherubic life on Earth, curbing the drive of the emotions through moral science, dispersing the darkness of reason through dialectics
Then may we imbue our purified and well-prepared soul with the light of natural philosophy so that afterward we may perfect it with the knowledge of things divine

judged.justification: Maps the Dionysian purgation, illumination and perfection onto moral philosophy, dialectics, natural philosophy and theology.

claims.text: Pico says the patriarch Jacob teaches through a figure that a ladder of many rungs stretches from the lowest earth to the highest heavens, with God at its height and the contemplative angels moving up and down it in turns.

quotes.text: let us also consult Jacob the patriarch

there is a ladder that stretches from the lowest earth to the highest Heavens and that is marked by a series of many rungs. God is at its height, and the contemplative angels move up and down it in turns
esse scalas ab imo solo ad caeli summa protensas, multorum graduum serie distinctas, fastigio Dominum insidere, contemplatores angelos per eas vicibus alternantes ascendere et descendere

claims.text: Pico asks who will dare touch the Ladder of God with unclean feet or unwashed hands, since it is unlawful to touch the clean with the unclean, when we try to imitate the angelic life.

quotes.text: if we are to carry out these things in our efforts to imitate the angelic life, who, I ask, will dare to touch the Ladder of God, either with unclean feet or with unwashed hands
It is unlawful, as the mysteries have it, to touch the clean with the unclean

claims.text: Pico says the sensual part of the soul must be washed in moral philosophy lest we be kept from the ladder, and that to be companions of the angels who run up and down Jacob's ladder we must also be prepared to move from step to step without leaving its course.

quotes.text: Let us wash them in moral philosophy as in a flowing river lest we be held back from the ladder as wicked and unclean
if we wish to be companions of the angels who hasten up and down Jacob's ladder unless we are first well prepared and instructed to be promoted from step to step

claims.text: Pico says that inspired by the cherubic spirit and philosophizing through the grades of nature, we descend and ascend in turn until we rest in the bosom of the Father, who is at the top of the ladder, and are made perfect in theological bliss.

quotes.text: Once we, inspired by the cherubic spirit, have reached this point through the art of speaking or of reasoning
until at last, resting in the bosom of the Father Who is at the top of the ladder, we shall be made perfect in theological bliss
iam Cherubico spiritu animati, per scalarum idest naturae gradus philosophantes

judged.justification: Makes the ladder of the angels the ladder of the grades of nature, climbed by philosophizing.

claims.text: Pico proposes to ask Job what God most desires among the tens of hundreds of thousands who assist Him, and says the answer will be peace.

quotes.text: And let us inquire of just Job, who entered into a living pact with the God of life before he was brought into being, as to what God the Highest desires among those tens of hundreds of thousands who are there present before Him. He will certainly answer “Peace,”
Percontemur et iustum Iob

claims.text: Pico says that the middle order interprets the precepts of the supreme order for the lower ones, and so has Empedocles interpret the words of the theologian Job.

quotes.text: And since the middle order interprets the precepts of the supreme order for the lower ones, let now Empedocles the philosopher interpret for us the words of Job the theologian
Et quoniam supremi ordinis monita medius ordo inferioribus interpretatur, interpretetur nobis Iob theologi verba Empedocles philosophus

judged.justification: States the mediating role of the middle order as a principle and applies it to philosophy between theology and the many.

claims.text: Pico says the peace that God makes in His heavens is the peace the descending angels announced to men of good will, so that men, ascending to heaven, would be transformed by it into angels.

quotes.text: that peace which God makes in His heavens, which the angels who came down to earth announced to men of good will so that these men would, ascending to heaven, be transformed by it into angels
ut per eam ipsi homines ascendentes in caelum angeli fierent

judged.justification: Names peace, and not only knowledge, as what turns men into angels.

claims.text: Pico says Moses is only a little inferior to the fountain of sacrosanct and ineffable intelligence whose nectar inebriates the angels.

quotes.text: Let us take as an example Moses, who is himself but a bit inferior to the fountain-like fullness of sacrosanct and ineffable intelligence whose nectar inebriates the angels
unde angeli suo nectare inebriantur

claims.text: Pico says that, raised to the heights of philosophy and roused by ineffable love, we shall be borne outside ourselves like ardent seraphim, filled with the godhead, no longer ourselves but He who made us.

quotes.text: roused by ineffable love as if by a frenzy, and borne outside ourselves like ardent seraphim, filled with the godhead, we shall no longer be ourselves, but He Himself Who made us
quasi Saraphini ardentes extra nos positi, numine pleni

judged.justification: Ties the seraphic state to the frenzy of love and to loss of the self in God.

claims.text: Pico says the noonday light of theology is the light that squarely enflames the seraphim and equally illuminates the cherubim.

quotes.text: This is the noonday light that squarely enflames the seraphim and equally illuminates the cherubim
Haec est illa lux meridialis quae Saraphinos ad lineam inflammat et Cherubinos pariter illuminat

claims.text: Pico says that, according to the doctrines of the cabalists and the Moors, there is no place for unclean spirits in the region of the noonday light.

quotes.text: This is the place where, according to the doctrines of the cabalists and the Moors, there is no place for unclean spirits

claims.text: Pico proposes that after the fall of our man, we call upon Raphael, the heavenly physician, to free us with moral philosophy and dialectics as healing drugs.

quotes.text: let us call upon Raphael, the heavenly physician, to set us free with moral philosophy and dialectics, as if with healing drugs
Raphaelem coelestem medicum advocemus, qui nos morali et dialectica uti pharmacis salutaribus liberet

judged.justification: Recasts the three philosophical stages as the offices of three archangels.

claims.text: Pico says that once restored to health Gabriel, the strength of God, will lead us through the marvels of nature and deliver us to Michael the high priest, who will bestow the insignia of theological priesthood.

quotes.text: Gabriel, the strength of God, will abide in us and, leading us through the marvels of nature and showing us everywhere the merit and the power of God, he will finally deliver us to Michael the high priest, who will in turn bestow upon us, who will have completed our service to philosophy, the insignia of theological priesthood
tandem sacerdoti summo Michaeli nos tradet

judged.justification: Assigns natural philosophy to Gabriel and theology to Michael, completing the archangelic sequence.

claims.text: Pico says that Esdras proclaimed of the seventy books that the fountain of wisdom is the exact metaphysics of the intelligible and angelic forms.

quotes.text: These tomes, as Esdras rightly proclaimed, clearly and from the outset, contain a vein of understanding
a font of wisdom that is the exact metaphysics of the intelligible and angelic forms
sapientiae fontem, idest de intelligibilibus angelicisque formis exactam metaphysicam

judged.justification: Says that angelic forms are the subject matter of the second of the three Kabbalistic disciplines.

claims.text: Pico says that in the Kabbalistic books he found the fall of the demons and the hierarchy of the angels, the same things read every day in Paul, Dionysius, Jerome and Augustine.

quotes.text: of the fall of the demons, of the hierarchy of the angels, of Purgatory, of the punishments in Hell. I saw the same things that we read every day in Paul, Dionysius, Jerome, and Augustine
de casu demonum, de ordinibus angelorum, de purgatoriis, de inferorum paenis eadem legi quae apud Paulum et Dionysium

judged.justification: Claims agreement between the Kabbalistic and the Christian angelology, the ground for reading the two hierarchies together.

claims.text: The editors report that Ficino's Platonic Theology places the soul between matter and angelic intelligences, while for Pico man's calling is the dynamism of transcending the world of images and becoming one with the Absolute rather than enjoying this central position.

quotes.text: This is also the central thesis of Marsilio Ficino's Platonic Theology, in which the soul is placed between matter and angelic intelligences

but Pico believes that man's calling consists not in the static enjoyment of this central position but rather in the dynamism by which the human being is called to transcend the world of images and finally to become one with the Absolute

bears_on.note: The note sets Pico's account of man's central place against Ficino's Platonic Theology.

judged.justification: Reads the Oration's opening as a departure from Ficino's static middle position.

claims.text: The editors note that the sequence sense, reason, intellect reappears in the three-stage ascent by the angelic orders, thrones, cherubim, seraphim, and that man is meant to transcend even the angelic orders.

quotes.text: Note the sequence sense, reason, intellect; these elements will reappear in the three-stage ascension according to the model of the angelic orders: thrones, cherubim, seraphim
where man is meant to transcend even the angelic orders and to become one with God

judged.justification: Reads the three-rank ladder as the ordering of the three faculties.

claims.text: The editors note an order of angels, stars, lower creatures in section 6 and say it is repeated in reverse order in section 11.

quotes.text: Note the order angels, stars, lower creatures, repeated in reverse order in §11

claims.text: The editors gloss the clause or soon thereafter in section 26 as meaning after Lucifer's fall.

quotes.text: That is, after Lucifer's fall

judged.justification: Supplies the referent of the clause 'or soon thereafter', which the text leaves unexplained.

claims.text: The editors adduce the Heptaplus second proem, where man's make-up is said to include the angelic mind and the image of God, as a parallel to the seeds of every kind of life.

quotes.text: In the second proem of Pico's Heptaplus (a commentary on Genesis), we read: “It is a common expression in the Schools to say that man is a microcosm, whose body is a mixture of elements, including the heavenly spirit, the vegetative soul, the senses of brutes, reason, the angelic mind and the image of God”

claims.text: The editors report that Bausi traces the passage on man's cultivating his seeds to Iamblichus.

quotes.text: In his commentary, Bausi (Pico 2003, 12–13, n29) traces this crucial passage to Iamblichus, Protrepticus 5

claims.text: The editors report that Garin points also to medieval sources for the passage, John of Salisbury and Alan of Lille.

quotes.text: Garin suggests looking to medieval sources as well, such as John of Salisbury (Policraticus 8.12 [PL 199.756b]) and Alan of Lille
the possibility for man to degenerate into a brute and regenerate himself in God are expressed in terms very similar to those used by Pico

claims.text: The editors report that Tognon proposes John Scotus Eriugena's De divisione naturae as the precise source of this whole section.

quotes.text: Tognon suggests a precise reference for this entire section of the Oratio: John Scotus Eriugena's De divisione naturae

claims.text: The editors report De Lubac's view that the Oration repeats an idea expressed many times before in patristic literature.

quotes.text: According to De Lubac, the Oration simply repeats the same idea that was expressed many times before in Patristic literature

claims.text: The editors cite Ficino's Platonic Theology 14.3, where the soul lives a life of plant, beast, man, hero, demon, angel and God, as a parallel to the passage.

quotes.text: Cf. Ficino, Theologia Platonica 14.3

the life of the demons insofar as it contemplates mathematics; the life of the angels insofar as it inquires into the mysteries divine; and the life of God insofar as it does all things for God's sake

bears_on.note: The editors put Ficino's ladder of lives, angels among them, beside Pico's scale of seeds.

claims.text: The editors report that Bori and Bausi suggest Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses among several plausible sources for the passage.

quotes.text: Among several plausible sources for this passage, both Bori (2000, 43) and Bausi (Pico 2003, 13) suggest Gregory of Nyssa (1978, Life of Moses 2.162–65)

claims.text: The editors report Copenhaver's remark that, apart from one exception, Pico's examples of mutability in this part of the Oration are negative and ambiguous, and that the only clearly positive transformation is angelic.

quotes.text: With one exception, Pico's other examples of mutability in this section of the Oration are as negative and ambiguous as the chameleon
The only clearly positive transformation is angelic” (Copenhaver 2002a, 60)

judged.justification: Isolates the angelic transformation as the one unambiguously positive change in the chameleon passage.

claims.text: The editors report that Garin and Tognon refer to the Ethiopic Book of Enoch 40.8 for the Enoch of this passage.

quotes.text: Both Garin and Tognon refer to the Ethiopic Book of Enoch 40.8 (first or second century; see Knibb 1978)

claims.text: The editors judge it more likely that Pico draws on a complex apocryphal tradition of Enoch texts than on a single book, and say the reference could include the Third Book of Enoch.

quotes.text: Rather than referring to a single text, Pico more likely elaborates on a complex, and apocryphal, textual tradition. His reference could include the so-called Third Book of Enoch

open_questions.text: Which Enoch text or texts Pico knew is not settled.

basis_quote.text: Pico more likely elaborates on a complex, and apocryphal, textual tradition

claims.text: The first printed edition leaves a blank where the Hebrew word should stand, and the two Basel editions supply a Hebrew retroversion of the Latin words angelum divinitatis instead.

quotes.text: The princeps edition has a blank space where the Hebrew word should be. Both Basel editions (1557 and 1572) have Mal'akh ha-Sekinach, Hebrew retroversion of the Latin angelum divinitatis

open_questions.text: What Hebrew word Pico wrote at this point is not fixed by the printed tradition, since the princeps has a blank and the Basel editions supply a back-translation.

basis_quote.text: The princeps edition has a blank space where the Hebrew word should be

judged.justification: The identification of the name as Metatron rests on a restoration, not on the printed text.

claims.text: The editors report that Bausi, following Wirszubski, restores the characters found in an earlier version of the Oration in a Florence manuscript and reads them as Metatron.

quotes.text: Following Wirszubski (1989, 232), Bausi (Pico 2003, 171–72) restores in his edition the characters found in the earlier version of the Oration (possibly one of two drafts Pico prepared in fall 1486 while in Umbria before moving to Rome) in the manuscript Palatino 885 of the National Library in Florence, reading them as Metatron

open_questions.text: Whether the characters of the earlier draft are what Pico intended for the printed text is left open by the note's hedge on the draft.

basis_quote.text: possibly one of two drafts Pico prepared in fall 1486

relations_local.basis: supplies a restoration for the blank the printed editions leave

judged.justification: Makes 'Metatron' a scholarly restoration from a manuscript, so the Enoch-Metatron reading of section 35 depends on the reading of a draft.

claims.text: The editors point to the Commento, which says almost in the exact terms of the Oration that Enoch was transformed into Metatron, angel of divinity, and that any other man may be transformed into an angel.

quotes.text: A reference to Metatron can be found in Pico's Commento sopra una canzona (written in the same period as the Oration and the Conclusiones, 1486) almost in the exact terms of the Oration, as a synonym of transfiguration

This is what the statement of the Cabalist wise men must mean, when they say that Enoch was transformed into Metatron, angel of divinity, or, in general, that any other man is transformed into an angel

claims.text: The editors direct readers to Conclusiones 1.19.2 and 2.11.10 for the interpretation of the Enoch-Metatron transfiguration.

quotes.text: On the interpretation of the Enoch-Metatron transfiguration, see also Conclusiones 1.19.2 (according to Themistius) and 2.11.10 (cabalistic conclusions confirming the Christian religion)

claims.text: The editors say it is generally held that the name Metatron has three possible etymologies: Greek Methathronius, one from a Hebrew word for watch, and one from metator, guide.

quotes.text: It is generally held that there are three possible etymological interpretations of the word Metatron: in addition to the Greek “Methathronius,” meaning he who is next to the throne of God, one derived from mat- ara (“keeper of the watch”), and one derived from metator (“guide”)

claims.text: The editors quote Scholem's account that two traditions were combined in the figure of Metatron, one of a heavenly angel created with the world and one that makes him Enoch, who ascended and was changed from a man into an angel.

quotes.text: As Scholem writes, “two different traditions have been combined in the figure of Metatron. One relates to the heavenly angel who was created with the creation of the world, or even before, and makes him responsible for performing the most exalted tasks in the heavenly kingdom
A different tradition associates Metatron with Enoch
he who ascended to heaven and was changed from a human being into an angel

claims.text: The editors quote Scholem's view that the tradition associating Metatron with Enoch is absent from the Talmud and the chief Midrashim because of the Talmudists' reluctance to regard Enoch favourably.

quotes.text: the fact that this second tradition associating Metatron with Enoch is “absent from the Talmud or the most important Midrashim, is evidently connected with the reluctance
of the Talmudists to regard Enoch in a favourable light” (Scholem, 1971–72, 1444–45)

claims.text: The editors say it is perhaps not surprising that the identification discussed in the note holds a prominent place in Pico's Christian Cabala.

quotes.text: It is perhaps not surprising that the identification occupies a prominent place in Pico's Christian Cabala

claims.text: The editors report that Bausi takes the passage to show that Pico does not hold metempsychosis and agrees with Ficino on a moral and allegorical reading of the transformations.

quotes.text: According to Bausi (Pico 2003, 17n37), this passage shows that Pico does not adhere to the doctrine of metempsychosis (or transmigration of the soul) and agrees with Ficino (Theol. Pl. 17.4) on a moral and allegorical interpretation of the transformations of which Empedocles and other ancient authors speak

bears_on.note: Bausi's reading places Pico with Ficino, Theologia Platonica 17.4, on allegorical transformations.

claims.text: The editors name Seneca, Aristotle and Dante as possible sources for the paragraph on the philosopher and the pure contemplator.

quotes.text: For this paragraph, possible sources are Seneca, Epistles 41.4–5, and Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 7.1 (1145a), echoed by Dante's Convivio 3.7.6

claims.text: The editors say that the words quoted from Ps. 81, You are gods and sons of the most high, were spoken by God to the angels condemned for their sins and are applied by Pico to men to incite them to rise toward an angelic form.

quotes.text: The reference is to Ps. 81:6–7

These are words spoken by God to the angels, condemned for their sins. Pico applies them to men in order to incite them to ascend from their intermediate (and shapeless) station toward a higher, angelic form

judged.justification: Shows Pico turning words addressed to fallen angels into an exhortation to ascend to the angelic state.

claims.text: The editors reject a previous translation of caelestia contemnamus as 'let us struggle toward the heavenly' and render it as spurn the celestial, keeping the classical sense of contemnare.

quotes.text: Wallis, Miller, and Carmichael mistakenly translate “caelestia contemnamus” as “let us struggle toward the heavenly.” I prefer to be consistent with the letter of the text, sticking to the classical meaning of the verb contemnare

open_questions.text: What Pico means by the celestial that is to be spurned is not settled.

basis_quote.text: Pico's reference might be to the astronomical-astrological knowledge of the heavens

judged.justification: Turns an exhortation to strive toward the heavens into a call to leave the celestial behind for the otherworldly court.

claims.text: The editors say that spurning the celestial is consistent with section 40, where Pico suggests a higher stage of contemplation beyond the earthly and the celestial.

quotes.text: In any case, it is consistent with what he writes in §40, where he suggests a higher stage of contemplation beyond the earthly and the celestial

claims.text: The editors note that the word dignity appears for the first time in the Oration at the passage on emulating the dignity and glory of the seraphim, cherubim and thrones.

quotes.text: This is the first time the word “dignity” appears in the text of the Oration

judged.justification: Locates the first use of 'dignity' in an exhortation to emulate the highest angels.

claims.text: The editors say that Pico represents here the three divisions of the highest order of angels according to the scheme of Pseudo-Dionysius, which Thomas and Gregory confirm.

quotes.text: In accordance with the scheme set out by Pseudo-Dionysius (see §70 of the Oration) and confirmed by St. Thomas (Summa Theologiae 1.108, art. 6) and St. Gregory (In evang. II hom. 34), Pico represents here the three divisions of the highest order of angels: the seraphim, the cherubim, and the thrones

claims.text: The editors say that calling the cherubim contemplators does not mean that the seraphim and thrones are not contemplators.

quotes.text: The fact that Pico specifically calls the cherubim contemplators does not, of course, mean that the seraphim and thrones are not

claims.text: The editors say that man's task is to emulate the highest angels and that dialectics is the necessary intermediate stage in the mystic process, citing Bori.

quotes.text: Man's task is the emulation of the highest angels, and dialectics is the necessary intermediate stage in this mystic process (Bori 1996b, 557)

claims.text: The editors report a suggestion, from Farmer, that Pico consciously overlaid the sefirot on the Dionysian hierarchy, so that seraphim correspond to Hesed, thrones to Din and cherubim to Binah.

quotes.text: It has been suggested (Farmer 1998, 346–51) that Pico consciously overlaid the cabalistic sefirot on the celestial hierarchy elucidated by Pseudo-Dionysius. In this arrangement, as it applies here, each of these three types of angels is associated with a specific sefirah: the seraphim with Hesed (love); the thrones with Din (judgment); the cherubim with Binah (intelligence)

open_questions.text: Whether Pico consciously overlaid the sefirot on the Dionysian ranks is put forward as a suggestion, not established.

basis_quote.text: It has been suggested (Farmer 1998, 346–51) that Pico consciously overlaid the cabalistic sefirot

judged.justification: If accepted, the three ranks carry Kabbalistic values (love, judgment, intelligence) alongside the Dionysian ones.

claims.text: The editors identify the passages in which Yahweh flies through the heavens mounted on a cherub as the background of God flying over the cherub.

quotes.text: Yahweh flies through the Heavens mounted on a cherub (2 Sam. 22:11; Ps. 17:11)

claims.text: The editors say Pico himself glosses the unusual image of God brooding in the Heptaplus, where the Spirit of the Lord that brooded is the spiritual Olympus, seat of the Spirits of the Lord, warming with its light.

quotes.text: This unusual phrase, in which God “broods,” is glossed by Pico himself in Heptaplus 2.2
that is, the closely adhering spiritual Olympus, the seat of the Spirits of the Lord, warmed it with its warmth-giving light

claims.text: The editors observe that the gloss of Ephrem, to which Pico's Heptaplus appeals for the sense brooded, says the thing that hovered over the waters was a normal wind and not the Spirit of the Lord.

quotes.text: Interestingly, the gloss of St. Ephrem in question (Com. on Genesis 1.7) explicitly states that it was a normal wind and not the Spirit of the Lord
as Hebrew wisdom has it and as Ephraim the Syrian translates it, 'brooded,' the Spirit of the Lord

claims.text: The editors report Bausi's note that most commentators cite Job 38:7 for the waters above the heavens that praise God, but Ps. 148:4 is a more likely source.

quotes.text: As Bausi rightly notes, most commentators direct the reader to Job 38:7, but a more likely source is actually Ps. 148:4

claims.text: The editors say that the seraphim, cherubim and thrones are known as the first hierarchy because they are closest to God.

quotes.text: These three classes of angels are known as the “first hierarchy,” as they are closest to God

claims.text: The editors say that the need for the middle level to join the upper and the lower is addressed in the Heptaplus in imagery consonant with this passage.

quotes.text: The necessity of the middle level in joining the upper and the lower is addressed in the Heptaplus (6.7) in imagery consonant with that employed here

claims.text: The editors say the Prime Minds are the angels and the Order of Pallas is a phrase referring to the cherubim, in so far as they preside over the contemplators, citing the 2003 commentary.

quotes.text: The “Prime Minds” are the angels; the “Order of Pallas” is a phrase referring to the cherubim, insofar as they preside over the contemplators (Pico 2003, 26–27)

judged.justification: Fixes the Order of Pallas as the cherubim, the contemplative rank.

claims.text: The editors cite Macrobius on the Dream of Scipio and Heptaplus 6.6 in the note on the section 66 phrase.

quotes.text: Cf. Macrobius, On the Dream of Scipio 1.6.11, and Pico's Heptaplus 6.6

claims.text: The editors report Bausi's view that the language of the wish to know what life the cherubim lead is drawn directly from Ermolao Barbaro.

quotes.text: Bausi (1996, 126) maintains that the language here is drawn directly from Ermolao Barbaro (1943, 1:15)

bears_on.note: Bausi, as reported, finds Barbaro's language in the Oration's passage on the cherubic life.

claims.text: The editors say the Dionysius of the Celestial Hierarchy was taken to be the follower of Paul mentioned in Acts.

quotes.text: Celestial Hierarchy 165b–c, 205c–209d. This Dionysius was, of course, thought to be the homonymous follower of Paul of Acts 17:34

claims.text: The editors say the mystic three-stage path was often articulated as purgatio, illuminatio, unitio or perfectio.

quotes.text: The mystic three-stage path, or triplex via, was often articulated as purgatio-illuminatio-unitio (or perfectio )

claims.text: The editors say that Augustine among others regularly defines the cherub as plenitudo scientiae, the fullness of knowledge.

quotes.text: Augustine, among several others, regularly defines the cherub as plenitudo scientiae (“the fullness of knowledge”)

claims.text: The editors suggest that Pico may also have been thinking of Richard of St. Victor's De arca mystica, where cherub means fullness of knowledge.

quotes.text: Pico may have also been thinking of Richard of St. Victor's De arca mystica

claims.hedge_words: Pico may have also been thinking

claims.text: The editors say that Richard of St. Victor's De duodecim patriarchis takes Jacob's twelve sons as the successive stages of the contemplator's quest for mystical enlightenment.

quotes.text: Richard of St. Victor's De duodecim patriarchis is based on the notion that Jacob was the father of twelve sons: the successive stages of the contemplator's quest for mystical enlightenment

claims.text: The editors say the topos of Jacob's image engraved in the throne of God comes from the Aggadic tradition.

quotes.text: The recurring topos of Jacob's image engraved in the throne of God comes from the Aggadic tradition. See Wolfson 1995, 1–62

claims.text: The editors say that Jacob saw God on earth only in a dream, while in heaven the vision of God is attainable in a waking state.

quotes.text: Jacob saw God here on Earth only during a dream (Gen. 28:11–17); in Heaven, however, the vision of God is attainable in a waking state

claims.text: The editors say that Pico's depiction of the relatively harmonious comings and goings of the angels on the ladder is a rather joyous contradiction of the typical iconography of the ladder.

quotes.text: Interestingly, Pico's depiction of the ... relatively harmonious comings and goings of the angels on the ladder is a rather joyous contradiction of the typical iconography of the ladder to God

judged.justification: Reads the angels' motion on the ladder as harmony against a tradition of struggle.

claims.text: The editors list Genesis 28:12-13, the Commento, Philo and Iamblichus as sources for the ladder.

quotes.text: Genesis 28:12–13; Commento (notes to sixth stanza); Philo, De somniis 1.2ff.; Iamblichus, Protrepticus 1 (41.11–24 in Iamblichus 1989)

claims.text: The editors identify Plato's Phaedo 67b as the source of the maxim that it is unlawful to touch the clean with the unclean.

quotes.text: See Plato, Phaedo 67b (Pico 2003, 31)

claims.text: The editors suggest that the passage on philosophizing from centre to centre may be inspired principally by al-Batalyawsi, citing Idel.

quotes.text: This passage may be inspired principally by al-Batalyawsi. See Idel (2005, Ascensions 183–87)

claims.text: The editors say the passage could refer to the metaphor of eternal happiness as circular movement, which the Heptaplus proem to book seven expresses.

quotes.text: This could be a reference to the metaphor of eternal happiness as circular movement

Circular motion, through which a body is carried around to the point from which it started, is the most express image of the true felicity, through which a creature returns to the beginning from which it proceeded

claims.text: The editors cite Job 25:2, Dan. 7:10, Gen. 1:2 and Heptaplus 3.6 for the passage on the multitude before God and the peace He makes in the heavens.

quotes.text: Job 25:2; Dan. 7:10; Gen. 1:2; Heptaplus 3.6. Cf. Conclusiones 1.28.24 (Farmer 1998, 355) and Mithridates (2005, 151)

claims.text: The editors cite Pseudo-Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy 209a-b, and Conclusiones 2.5.3 for the middle order interpreting the precepts of the supreme order for the lower.

quotes.text: Pseudo-Dionysius, Celestial Hierarchy 209a–b. Cf. Conclusiones 2.5.3

claims.text: The editors cite Luke 2:13-14 and Heptaplus 7.4 for the angels who announced peace to men.

quotes.text: Cf. Luke 2:13–14 and Heptaplus 7.4

claims.text: The editors say the image of heavenly nectar goes back to Plato's account of the angelic charioteer who refreshes his horses with ambrosia and nectar.

quotes.text: The image of heavenly nectar in this context goes back to Plato's discussion of the angelic charioteer who, after guiding the soul to heaven, refreshes his horses with ambrosia and nectar (Phaedrus 243e–257a)

claims.text: The editors judge it probable that Pico starts from the Platonic notion of nectar in heaven and adds the reference to intoxication through Plotinus's reading of the Symposium, where it means the passing down of knowledge from higher to lower levels.

quotes.text: Pico probably begins with this Platonic notion of the presence of nectar in heaven but then, relying on Plotinus's interpretation (Enneads 3.5.9) of a passage in Plato's Symposium (203b–c), adds the reference to intoxication, an allusion in the case of Plotinus to the way in which knowledge is passed down from higher to lower levels

claims.text: The editors cite Philo for the cherub as the supercelestial charioteer who guides the soul in an orderly fashion away from discord.

quotes.text: For the cherub as the supercelestial charioteer who guides the soul in an orderly fashion away from discord, see Philo, On the Cherubim 23–24

claims.text: The editors tie the ardent seraphim of section 113 to sections 54 and 57 and to Ficino's De divino furore.

quotes.text: On the ardent seraphim, cf. §§54 and 57. See, again, Ficino's De divino furore (in Ficino 1576, 613)

bears_on.note: The note sets the seraphic frenzy beside Ficino's De divino furore.

claims.text: The editors give Gregory the Great's XL Homiliarum in Evangelia as a possible source of this angelological passage, in which Raphael is called the medicine of God.

quotes.text: For a possible source of this angelological conclusion, see Gregory the Great, XL Homiliarum in Evangelia libri duo 34.9 (PL 76.1251a): “Raphael vero dicitur medicina Dei”

claims.text: The editors give the same work of Gregory the Great for the meanings of the names Gabriel, strength of God, and Michael, who is like God.

quotes.text: Cf. Gregory the Great, XL Homiliarum in Evangelia libri duo 34.9 ( PL 76.1251a): “Gabriel autem, fortitudo Dei”
Cf. Gregory the Great, XL Homiliarum in Evangelia libri duo 34.9 ( PL 76.1251a):“Michael namque, qui ut Deus”

claims.text: The editors say that a connection between the names of the angels and the doctrine of the sefirot, for which they cite Yates, might be alluded to through the words the most hidden mysteries.

quotes.text: On the names of the angels as connected to the doctrine of the sefirot (a connection which might be alluded to through the words “the most hidden mysteries”), see Yates (1979)

judged.justification: Suggests the three archangels' names carry a Kabbalistic sense.

claims.text: The editors say Pico identifies Michael, the high priest, with the sefirah Keter, which he takes as the symbol of the priesthood.

quotes.text: See also §141, “sacerdoti summo Michaeli” in reference to the archangel, whose name in Hebrew translates as “Who is like God?”
Michael with the sefirah Keter (Crown), which he interprets as the symbol of the priesthood

judged.justification: Gives the archangel Michael a place in the sefirotic scheme, beyond the Dionysian one.

claims.text: The editors say that the order of Pallas is described as cherubic contemplation that fulfils the link between love, the seraphim, and justice or law, the thrones.

quotes.text: See §161 and §§65–66, where “the order of Pallas” is described as that of cherubic contemplation that brings to fruition the link between love (the seraphim) and justice or law (the thrones)

judged.justification: Reads the cherub as joining love and judgment, so Pallas names the mediating rank.

claims.text: The editors say Pallas signifies the intellectual nature which leads to wisdom and that the Orphean Pallas is associated with the cabalists' Metatron in Conclusiones 2.5.14 and 2.11.10.

quotes.text: throughout the Oration and Conclusiones, as the personification of Wisdom or Philosophy, Pallas signifies the intellectual nature which leads to wisdom (in Conclusiones 2.5.14 and 2.11.10, the Orphean Pallas is associated with the cabalists' Metatron)

judged.justification: Links the Order of Pallas of section 66 to Metatron, so the cherubic order and the Enoch of section 35 may name one figure.

claims.text: The editors say the archangel Uriel appears to Esdras in a vision and that Esdras writes down the angelic revelations in seventy books.

quotes.text: the archangel Uriel appears in a vision to Esdras, who transcribes the angelic revelations in seventy books
the seventh and final vision that Esdras has under visitation of the angel Uriel explicitly states that Esdras composed seventy books of esoteric revelations

claims.text: The editors say the three archangels Pico mentions represent dialectics, natural philosophy and theology, and give the section number as 135.

quotes.text: The three archangels Pico mentions in §135 represent dialectics, natural philosophy, and theology

claims.text: The editors report Tognon's phrase that at this point in the first redaction of the Oration Pico underwent an intellectual conversion to the Cabala.

quotes.text: It is at this point in the first redaction of the oration that Pico underwent what Tognon refers to as an “intellectual conversion” (in Pico 1987, 65n16) to the Cabala

judged.justification: Dates Pico's turn to the Cabala to the passage on the angelic forms in the earlier redaction.

claims.text: The editors say the passage of section 240 recalls the image of Jacob and the ladder and that Moses instructs us to prepare for a heavenly vision through philosophy.

quotes.text: This passage recalls the image of Jacob and the ladder (§§73–74). Moses instructs us to prepare for a heavenly vision through the study of philosophy (§102)

not_mined: Oration passages not about angels or the ascent: sections 1-2, 7-10, 12-13, 16-25, 31-34, 38, 41-47, 58, 60 (except as the waters above the heavens in the footnote on section 60), 77-79, 85-94, 96-97, 99-112 (except 98 and 113), 114-136, 138, 142-249 and 251-264 except 250 and 254; the footnotes on the Empedocles and Osiris passages, the Chaldean Oracles and Zoroaster (sections 43-44, 130-134), the four furores (sections 109-112, 113 apart from the seraphim), the Pythagorean symbols (sections 116-129), and the disputation apparatus.
Sections 108-110 (Phaedrus frenzy, whisked away to the heavenly Jerusalem) are about the ascent but not the angelic state; left for a packet on the ascent.
Footnote 101 (Macarius, the hand beneath the cherub's wings, grace and the soul as God's throne) is only marginally angelological; not extracted.

The introductions of the edition (Riva, Bori, Papio) are not in the OCR file, which begins at Part II, the text; a claim from the editors' introduction on the erased word 'demon' (cited in footnote 46) could not be checked.

proposed_topics.label: The Oration's ascent to the angelic state and beyond it: sections 29-30, 37-40, 95, 113; stages of purgation, illumination and perfection
The archangels Raphael, Gabriel and Michael (and Uriel) in Oration sections 140-141 and the editors' notes
Jacob's ladder and the angels on it in the Oration (sections 73-82, 240)

notes:
GATE: the 70 editorial claims (attribution scholar_claim or scholar_report, quotes from the editors' footnotes in borghesi2012) initially raised the error scholar_from_primary because borghesi2012 is in PRIMARY_WORKS; the verifier was since revised so that quoting the editors' notes is allowed and gives only a warning (scholar_from_edition, 91 of them, all expected). Each such quotation was chosen from a footnote, not from Pico's text. Attribution was never changed to primary_text to satisfy the gate.

Cruxes and observations. (1) Section 35: the princeps has a blank where the Hebrew word stands; the Basel editions give a Hebrew retroversion of angelum divinitatis (Mal'akh ha-Sekinach); Bausi, following Wirszubski, restores the characters of the earlier draft in Palatino 885 and reads Metatron (footnote 34). Claims 054-055 record this. The Hebrew characters in the Latin/English line are quoted as OCR gives them. (2) Footnote 357 says the three archangels are mentioned 'in section 135'; the archangels are named in sections 140-141 (section 135 is Zoroaster's rivers and the four directions). Recorded as the editors state it; a reader should treat the section number as probably wrong. (3) Footnote 12 says the order angels, stars, lower creatures in section 6 is 'repeated in reverse order' in section 11; recorded as stated. (4) Footnote 52 and footnote 60 give two different framings of the three highest ranks (Dionysian first hierarchy; Farmer's sefirot overlay: seraphim Hesed, thrones Din, cherubim Binah); they do not contradict each other but the second is hedged ('It has been suggested'). (5) The Order of Pallas: footnote 60 says it means the cherubim; footnote 185 says Pallas is associated with Metatron in Conclusiones 2.5.14 and 2.11.10, which ties section 66 to section 35; a linker should connect these. (6) The editors quote Pico's Heptaplus and Commento in their own translation in footnotes 25, 54 and 77; those are recorded as editorial adductions (scholar_claim), not as primary_text. (7) Latin in the printed text is quoted where the wording matters; lines in the Latin pages are OCR with hyphenated line breaks (gate copes). (8) theses is left empty: the footnotes cite Conclusiones by Pico's section numbers (for example 2.11.10, 1.19.2), and the mapping to Farmer's ids in data/inventory/theses.json was not verified. (9) Audit leads: sections 5, 11, 29, 30, 35, 59-66, 82, 95, 140-141 and notes about 25-27, 33-34, 60, 69 confirmed and extracted. Section 131 and notes 163-164 (Zoroaster's winged soul) are not about angels and were left out. Passages the audit missed and added: sections 3-6, 14-15, 26, 37, 39-40, 46, 48-57, 61-62, 67-72, 75-76, 80-81, 83-84, 98, 113, 137, 139, 250, 254, and notes 7, 8, 12, 24, 25, 27, 28, 37, 45, 46, 49, 52-55, 59, 61, 64, 66-70, 77, 83, 97, 107, 136, 175-177, 185, 327, 337, 352, 356, 357.
